items.title: EEG Correlates of Verbal and Perceptual Reasoning
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Gwyneth Rolph
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying the neural underpinnings of intelligence is one of the major goals of modern intelligence research. However, few imaging studies explore the high extremes of intelligence, and most use only a single composite IQ score. This study used quantitative EEG recordings to investigate correlations between the EEG variables of individual alpha peak frequency, relative power, and coherence, and scores on verbal and perceptual reasoning tests in participants with IQs from the low-average to exceptionally gifted ranges. Overall, the results did not reveal any pattern of significant relationships between these EEG measures and the two psychometric tests. Since this study had only a small sample, heavily skewed towards the high-IQ end of the scale, no definitive conclusions about the EEG measures and verbal and perceptual reasoning can be drawn. Nevertheless, it reveals many opportunities for further research, and suggestions are made for progressing this topic in the future.

items.title: State Space Models Naturally Produce Time Cell and Oscillatory Behaviors and Scale to Abstract Cognitive Functions
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Sen Lu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Mingtao Hu, Eric Yeu-Jer Lee, Soohyeon Kim, Wei D. Lu
items.summary: arXiv:2507.13638v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A grand challenge in modern neuroscience is bridging the gap between the microscale neural circuits and cognitive functions. While extensive knowledge exists about neuronal connectivity and biophysics, how low-level phenomena give rise to abstract behaviors remains largely unresolved. Here, we propose that a mathematical framework based on State Space Models offers mathematical sufficiency and computational plausibility to generate response profiles that resemble time cells, ramping activity, and oscillatory responses. Our results suggest that such behaviors can emerge from a structured multi-timescale complex rotational basis, which enables optimized history compression and naturally generates structured temporal dynamics even prior to training, mirroring recent findings in biological circuits. Learning exploits and adapts to the pre-existing temporal basis for specific tasks. We show that the model can readily scale to abstract cognitive functions such as event counting, supporting its use as a computationally tractable framework for understanding neural activities.

items.title: Simulation Based Inference of a Simple Neural Network Structure
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Pierre Charitat (IRMA), S\'egolen Geffray (IRMA), Christophe Pouzat (IRMA)
items.summary: arXiv:2604.18599v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neurophysiologists are nowadays able to record from a large number of extracellular electrodes and to extract, from the raw data, the sequences of action potentials or spikes generated by many neurons. Unfortunately these ''many neurons'' still represent only a tiny fraction of the neuronal population that constitutes the network. Using association statistics such as the estimation of the cross-correlation functions, they are trying to infer the structure of the network formed by the recorded neurons. But this inference is compromised by the tremendous under-sampling of the neuronal population. We propose to focus instead on simple spike train statistics, like the empirical spikes frequency, or the interspike interval distribution. Their sampling distributions can be estimated by simulations, and, given a few observed spike train statistics, they provide enough information to infer the structure of the underlying network. We show that, on a ''toy model'', our method gives significantly better results than the sub-network reconstruction method with regards to the inference of the connection probability of the original network.

items.title: Position: Hippocampal Explicit Memory Is the Cornerstone for AGI
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Sangjun Park
items.summary: arXiv:2606.11245v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, raising expectations for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). This position paper argues that integrating explicit memory is the cornerstone for advancing LLMs toward AGI. The key reason is that the underlying learning mechanism of LLMs is highly analogous to human implicit memory. However, higher-order cognitive functions necessary for AGI, such as long-term strategic planning, metacognition, and symbolic reasoning, heavily rely on hippocampal explicit memory and cannot arise solely from implicit statistical learning. Drawing on findings from neuroscience, I advance this perspective and complement it with computational requirements for artificial explicit memory systems, hoping to foster further research and lay the groundwork for explicit memory integration.

items.title: NeuronDiscover: Agent-in-Twin for Mechanistic Discovery in Neuronal Microenvironments with World Action Models
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Haowei Xu, Wanyi Fu, Hongbin Han, Zhaoheng Xie
items.summary: arXiv:2609.35338v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mechanistic discovery in neuronal microenvironments requires interventions and measurements that separate competing explanations of solute transport and neuronal response. Predictive accuracy cannot settle the question: a real mechanistic change and an error in the computational twin leave the same signature in sparse observations. We formalize this twin confounding and reason over a joint mechanism--discrepancy belief, designing experiments that separate the two. NeuronDiscover is an Agent-in-Twin framework whose shared, mechanism-grounded World Action Model (WAM) couples prediction, intervention proposals, and observation design; independently adjudicated outcomes revise a scoped Mechanism--Intervention--Observation--Outcome (MIOY) graph, whose supported relations compile into executable programs carrying discrepancy-adjusted acceptance bounds. We evaluate on simulated brain-fluid tracer-transport worlds adjudicated by an independently frozen finer-mesh reference solver, and on donor-disjoint public current-clamp recordings of cortical neurons. Counting only relations that reach a certified terminal status, and scoring abstentions as unresolved for every method, at a matched budget of 16 experiments over 32 source units NeuronDiscover resolves 4.0 relations per assigned world against 3.4 for the strongest baseline and 3.2 without graph revision, at 5% false support and 82% scope accuracy. Joint mechanism--discrepancy acquisition resolves 3.8 relations versus 2.9 for plug-in expected information gain; discrepancy-adjusted verification lowers accepted-program failure from 15% to 9% at 60% acceptance coverage; and transfer to the recordings yields 1.94 versus 1.53 relations per assigned world. Correctness is adjudicated within declared model worlds and archival recordings.

items.title: NeuronSifter: An Agent-in-Twin for Prioritizing Central Nervous System Interventions with World Action Models
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Haowei Xu, Wanyi Fu, Hongbin Han, Zhaoheng Xie
items.summary: arXiv:2609.35445v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Effective central nervous system (CNS) intervention requires more than predicting biological responses: a scientific system must determine which intervention, observation, or additional evidence can improve a decision under uncertainty. However, in partially observed neuronal microenvironments, identical predicted outcomes may correspond to different exposure states, biological mechanisms, and intervention risks. We propose NeuronSifter, a decision-centric Agent-in-Twin framework, where an AI agent operates with an evolving biological digital twin rather than a fixed predictive model. NeuronSifter compiles interventions into state-conditional target-occupancy representations, propagates them through a mechanism-grounded World Action Model (WAM), and selects informative measurements based on their expected reduction in decision uncertainty. A shared probabilistic belief state couples intervention simulation, observation selection, and outcome assimilation, enabling the digital twin to continuously refine its decision-relevant representations through externally verified evidence. We evaluate NeuronSifter in Alzheimer's disease intervention scenarios using mechanistic neuronal microenvironment simulations and retrospective clinical endpoint references. The evaluation framework examines adaptive evidence acquisition, uncertainty-aware intervention planning, and robustness under model discrepancy through controlled environments and independent comparisons. NeuronSifter demonstrates how an AI system can actively identify missing evidence, refine biological hypotheses, and optimize intervention decisions under limited experimental budgets. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/NeuronSifter.

items.title: Simulating Alzheimer's amyloid-like pathology on a fly central nervous system connectome
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Taeho Jo
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, the amount of pathology in the brain is an imperfect predictor of how much function is lost. Pathology leads to that loss through neural circuits, but these cannot be observed neuron by neuron in patients. This study therefore simulated the central nervous system of the adult male Drosophila melanogaster: 166,700 integrate-and-fire neurons wired by the MaleCNS connectome. The simulator reproduced a published fly brain model (rate correlation 0.9997). Three kinds of damage reported in amyloid-$\beta$ flies, a lowered spike threshold, synapse loss and neuron loss, were imposed with assumed magnitudes, and circuit responses were measured in 1,424 simulated flies. The number of neurons lost was a poor guide to the deficit, which depended partly on how many synaptic contacts went with them and whether they included input neurons or one command neuron. With the same 12% of neurons removed, odour-evoked whole-brain activity was 93%, 47% or 31% of the healthy value when damage fell on poorly connected, random or highly connected neurons; these flies lost 20%, 35% and 48% of contacts. When the contacts lost were equalised, the three groups differed less; whether the remaining difference reflects where the damage fell could not be established. In 48 flies, restoring only the contacts that surviving neurons had lost recovered 62% of the whole-brain deficit, and restoring the removed neurons 39%. In flies that had lost neurons delivering the odour, these accounted for about half the deficit due to neuron loss. One neuron could decide an outcome: all 66 flies that lost the giant fibre on the stimulated side, which commands escape, had a giant fibre rate below 100 Hz, against 1 of 254 that kept it. Whole-brain activity revealed damage at milder severity than the learning index, because it changed much relative to its variation between trials.

items.title: Effects of cortisol time-scales in a model of emotion regulation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Michael Buccino, Joshua Ginart, Eva Kaslik, Anca Radulescu
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stress reshapes cortico-limbic dynamics across multiple timescales, with important consequences for healthy and pathological arousal responses. We develop and analyze a Wilson-Cowan model of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry, incorporating excitatory and inhibitory populations involved in emotional regulation. The effects of stress cortisol are represented as history-dependent modulations of two stress-sensitive interactions: recurrent prefrontal excitation and inhibition of basolateral amygdala principal cells. Using numerical simulations and bifurcation analysis, we examine how this self-interacting system organizes transitions between stable activity and infra-slow oscillations, and how this structure changes with cortisol-related temporal memory. To distinguish the effects of memory temporal distribution from those of its timescale, we compare weak and strong Gamma kernels with a discrete-delay limit, representing progressively different ways in which past activity can influence current coupling. Introducing temporal memory reshapes the parameter region supporting oscillations and alters their persistence. Weak and strong Gamma kernels produce remarkably similar global dynamics, whereas the discrete-delay limit generates a substantially richer bifurcation structure, including quasiperiodic activity. Together, these results suggest that the dynamical effects of cortisol depend not only on the characteristic timescale of its action, but also on the shape of the temporal memory through which past neural activity influences the present. Different forms of temporal integration may provide a mechanism by which neural systems implement distinct functional dynamics, while changes in this integration could promote atypical or pathological rhythmic regimes.

items.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Nima Dehghani
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

items.title: Reciprocity coordinates a three-way trade-off in recurrent neural circuits
items.subtitle: ARXIV · Q-BIO.NC · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Xiaoyu Zhang, Mingyi Huang, Yixuan Cui, Xin Lu, Yuguo Yu
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biological neural circuits contain both unidirectional and reciprocal connections, but how reciprocity affects circuit computation remains unclear. We varied reciprocity \r{ho} across 21 levels in recurrent-network simulations while holding network size, connection density, and directed-edge count fixed. Low-reciprocity networks produced more diverse stimulus-driven activity and performed better on four continuous-input tasks, whereas higher reciprocity generally improved performance on three delayed-memory tasks. Increasing reciprocity reduced online memory capacity and accelerated recovery from perturbations. A post-cue noise experiment showed that higher reciprocity suppressed internal noise propagation but made cue-evoked states less distinguishable, and component matching separated the contributions of cue separation and within-cue dispersion to readout robustness. Within this ensemble, reciprocity thus mediates a three-way trade-off among representational capacity, local stability, and task-state separability: higher reciprocity lowers capacity, strengthens stability, and compresses separability. Whether it improves behaviour depends on whether the stability gain outweighs the lost separation between task states. Connectome and microcircuit datasets from five species showed intermediate reciprocity, while reciprocity varied substantially across adult Drosophila brain regions, providing compatible structural context and motivating circuit-specific functional tests.

items.title: Hyperentanglement in intermediate phase-space planes: benchmarking a photon-pair source for quantum key distribution
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Murilo H. Magiotto, Millena B. Novaes, Wesley B. Cardoso, Ardiley T. Avelar, 1 Paulo H. Souto Ribeiro, Stephen P. Walborn, Guilherme L. Zanin, Rafael M. Gomes
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize a source of photon pairs simultaneously entangled in polarization and in the transverse spatial degree of freedom, with the spatial measurements performed in intermediate planes of the fractional Fourier transform. The source consists of two crossed type-I crystals in a non-collinear geometry, such that the transverse variables carry information about the crystal of origin. Detection in the crystal plane reveals this information completely and destroys the polarization entanglement, so that a scheme using the near and far fields as conjugate spatial bases cannot support a parallel polarization channel. In intermediate planes both spatial bases combine position and momentum, such that the which-crystal information is partially erased, and the polarization entanglement survives in all four combinations of spatial bases. Applying Bell and Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen criteria to the same photon pairs certifies both degrees of freedom simultaneously. We evaluate quantum bit error rates and asymptotic secret key rates in each degree of freedom, and find that the source delivers two simultaneously usable channels per photon pair.

items.title: Multi-Instantons and Exact-WKB Stokes Jumps in Multi-Well Quantum Mechanics
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Alireza Behtash, Syo Kamata
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the relation between the exact-WKB Delabaere--Dillinger--Pham Stokes jumps and the multi-instanton expansion of a one-dimensional potential with $N$ equal-depth minima. For a single barrier this relation is the Bogomolny--Zinn-Justin cancellation between the instanton--anti-instanton ambiguity and the Borel ambiguity of perturbation theory, and we extend it to every consecutive barrier interval and to the integration contours themselves. In the dilute large-$T$ regime at fixed nonperturbative grade, we derive the quasi-zero mode integral over the instanton separations from the Euclidean path integral and reduce it to Gamma and Hankel periods. With the local Weber level function of each well and one normalization per well fixed by the local Weber connection matrix, these periods reproduce the two lateral connected exact-WKB coefficients. The two lateral contours of each instanton--anti-instanton separation differ by exactly one Hankel cycle, and this linear Picard--Lefschetz relation reproduces the Stokes jump of the connected coefficient. A numerical solution of the Schr\"odinger equation for a symmetric triple well confirms the resulting two-barrier level splitting. At higher fixed grade, the map from ordered event sequences to normalized scalar coefficient products is not one-to-one. At leading dilute order the scalar weight of a closed event sequence depends only on the numbers of barrier crossings, $\mathcal I\bar{\mathcal I}$ pairs, and $\mathcal I\mathcal I$/$\bar{\mathcal I}\bar{\mathcal I}$ pairs. We construct two inequivalent grade-six triple-well event sequences with the same product of local Weber amplitudes, which embed in every potential with $N\ge3$ wells. Our results hold within the regular dilute, one-loop, local Weber approximation.

items.title: Deterministic and Programmable Fusion for Scalable Generation of Photonic Graph States
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Yan Li, Yunfan Yang, Zenghui Bao, Jize Yang, Luyan Sun, Yipu Song, Yukai Wu, Hongyi Zhang, Luming Duan
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement in multiphoton graph states is an important resource with various applications, such as measurement-based quantum computing and memory-less quantum repeaters. While some primitive instances have been successfully prepared, scalable generation of large-scale graph states with programmable connections remains an outstanding challenge. Fusion provides a promising "divide-and-conquer" approach by linking smaller resource states into larger, more complex graphs. However, its practical scalability has been limited by the probabilistic nature of conventional fusion protocols, which necessitates extensive hardware overhead and feed-forward resources to achieve deterministic outcomes. Here, we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a deterministic fusion operation with built-in error mitigation, capable of connecting small time-bin-encoded cluster states--originally generated on-demand from a quantum emitter--into larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states of increased sizes. The fusion operation is realized by nondestructively projecting pairs of flying microwave photonic qubits into Bell states using superconducting circuits with in-situ programmability. items.title: Photon Demultiplexing Using Spatial Routing
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hashir Kuniyil, Asad Ali, Saif Al-Kuwari
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial sectioning of the far-field noncollinear field from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is a promising approach for multiparty quantum communication. Although demonstrations with six pairs of users have been reported, the fundamental limits remain unknown. These include the maximum number of channels, the required degree of channel optimization, and the dependence on input parameters. In this paper, we provide a practical framework that answers these questions by connecting input parameters and invoking a design theorem. For a representative configuration, we realize 12 user-pair channels with routing consistency exceeding $0.9999$ at a $12\%$ reduction in photon flux. We further show that sectioning improves the accidental-coincidence budget linearly with the number of channels $N$, allowing the aggregate key rate to scale with the user count. These results provide a design strategy for spatial-division multiplexing of entangled photons analogous to the channel-spacing standards used in wavelength-division networks.

items.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for R\'enyi Entropies Estimation
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zongxing Xiong, Chengshen Gao, Lvzhou Li
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entropy estimation of discrete probability distributions is a fundamental problem in statistical inference and quantum property estimation. In this paper, we study the problem of estimating R\'enyi entropy $H_\alpha(\mathbf{p})$ for any distribution $\mathbf{p} = (p_i)_{i=1}^n$ given its purified quantum query-access. We also strengthen the precision-dependent lower bound to $\Omega\big(1/\epsilon^{\max\{1,1/(2\alpha)\}}\big)$ for $0<\alpha<1$, which identifies the optimal precision dependence of our algorithm.

items.title: Joint-measurement advantage and finite-time transitions in accelerated detector registers
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zhiming Huang
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Unruh response thermalizes accelerated detectors, but the entanglement remaining in a register does not by itself specify what distributed measurements can recover. We study this distinction for a four-qubit cluster state whose two assisting nodes independently undergo generalized amplitude damping, while the target nodes remain isolated and the environments are inaccessible. We derive the exact joint-assisted concurrence and the exact one-way value for arbitrary local measurements. The joint optimum equals the bipartition negativity, and computational-basis measurements attain the one-way optimum. A polar-decomposition argument, together with compactness, establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for separable measurements to attain the joint optimum and proves a strict gap whenever this condition fails. For assisting detectors at equal Unruh temperature with relaxation-rate ratio $r>1$, joint advantage exists precisely when the thermal excitation factor satisfies $q<1/r$. At finite positive temperature it ends at a unique finite time, while the remaining entanglement is nonzero. For $r=2$, both the transition time and remaining resource have closed expressions. These results identify when joint assistance is necessary within the independent weak-coupling thermalization model.

items.title: Testing graph isomorphism using simple quantum circuits
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Samuel Beasley, Ashley Montanaro
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The graph isomorphism problem asks whether two graphs are equivalent up to a permutation of their vertices. Its precise computational complexity remains unresolved, and it is still unknown whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists. We investigate whether simple graph-dependent Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) and Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) circuits can distinguish non-isomorphic graphs. We first show that suitable IQP and QAOA constructions allow the underlying graph to be reconstructed using a polynomial number of samples. Building on previous work using the QAOA energy, we show that Hamming weight distributions can distinguish graph pairs at circuit depths for which the numerically computed energy gap is zero. We then apply graph invariants to the matrix of ZZ correlators on the output distribution. For the specific case of the graph spectrum, at QAOA depth $p=2$, this invariant numerically distinguishes all $10{,}486$ cospectral regular graph pairs tested on up to 18 vertices. For IQP circuits, we introduce a finer invariant based on probability multiplicities within Hamming weight sectors, which distinguishes every non-isomorphic graph pair tested numerically. Finally, we derive exact graph-theoretic characterisations of the IQP output distribution at $\theta=\pi/2$ and $\theta=\pi/4$. These results show that simple graph-dependent quantum circuits encode substantial structural information, while leaving open whether this information can be extracted efficiently for general graph isomorphism.

items.title: Trading energy for coherence in mode discrimination
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shuyang Meng, Valerio Scarani
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy is arguably the main resource in classical physics; coherence is the prototypical quantum resource. In this paper, we study the interplay between these two resources in the task of optimal mode discrimination. This task, motivated by cryptography and metrology, consists of finding in which mode a signal has been encoded, for a given finite set of possible modes. After recalling that the task can be cast as a semi-definite program, we solve completely the case of two-mode discrimination under a hard energy constraint $n\leq N$. Specifically, we identify the region of modes overlap, for which the maximal energy state (the Fock state with N excitations) is the best choice for discrimination. For other overlaps, having access to coherence leads to better discrimination.

items.title: Single and coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators: Wigner-function dynamics, exact qutrit solutions, and synchronization
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rohitashwa Chattopadhyay, Vinayak Pendse, Shamik Gupta
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantum van der Pol oscillator in which single-photon pumping competes with a nonlinear two-photon dissipative channel to produce a quantum limit cycle, and the question of how two such oscillators with non-identical intrinsic frequencies synchronize in the sense of phase locking when coupled dissipatively to one another. For a single oscillator, starting from a Lindblad description of the dynamics, we derive the exact Wigner-function evolution equation, and show that its Fokker--Planck approximation admits in the appropriate regime an equivalent classical It\^{o} stochastic description that reproduces remarkably well the full Lindblad dynamics. Notably, the stochastic approach provides an efficient means of capturing system dynamics in the semiclassical regime, where a large number of energy eigenstates contribute and direct numerical simulations become computationally demanding. Restricting to the three lowest Fock states and using a parity symmetry, we obtain in closed form the stationary-state density matrix and its Wigner-function representation that displays pronounced nonclassical features. For two non-identical oscillators, we study the full Lindblad dynamics numerically and characterize synchronization through the stationary-state order parameter as a function of frequency mismatch and dissipative coupling. We find that increasing the effective nonlinear dissipative strength suppresses the synchronized region. Restricting the two oscillators to the three-level qutrit subspace, a parity symmetry reduces the stationary-state problem to an exact $41$-dimensional linear system, allowing to compute the synchronization order parameter. In this reduced description, results in the limit of large dissipation agree closely with those from the full dynamics, while exhibiting in the limit of small dissipation a double-peak synchronization structure accompanied by a phase reversal.

items.title: On the structure of low-rank PPT entangled states violating Peres conjecture
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Gurvir Singh, Manik Banik
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bound-entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT) can exhibit quantum steering and Bell nonlocality, disproving the long-standing Peres conjecture and its stronger steering counterpart. These counterexamples, obtained through explicit constructions or numerical searches, raise the question of whether they share a common structural origin. We address this question in the low-rank regime by asking whether known counterexamples can be obtained, up to invertible local filtering, from the complement of an unextendible product basis (UPB). We find that the answer depends crucially on the local dimension. In $3\otimes3$, the rank-four structure of PPT entangled states implies that both the steerable PPT state of Moroder \textit{et al.} and the Bell-nonlocal PPT state of V\'ertesi and Brunner can be obtained from UPB-complement states under invertible local filtering. For three qubits, in contrast, rank-four states that are PPT across every bipartition are separable across each cut. Moreover, comparison of the product-vector structure of the relevant kernels shows that the known three-qubit Bell-nonlocal PPT states cannot be obtained by invertible local filtering from the complement of any three-qubit UPB. Going beyond rank four, we further show that a known rank-eight three-qutrit state, supported on the complement of a UPB and PPT across every bipartition, is genuinely multipartite entangled. These results show that UPBs provide a unifying structural origin for important low-rank PPT entangled states in $3\otimes3$, but that nonlocal bound entanglement is not, in general, a UPB phenomenon.

items.title: Quantum Folding in Chebyshev-Based Quantum Subspace Diagonalization
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Seung Park, Dongni Chen, Stefano Chesi, Kyunghyun Baek, Mahn-Soo Choi
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum subspace diagonalization (QSD) with a Krylov space spanned by Chebyshev polynomials of the Hamiltonian is a natural ground-state method for fault-tolerant quantum computers, but every guarantee it offers---convergence rate, noise floor, and the cost of turning its classical output back into a physical state---is controlled by the overlap of the reference state with the true ground state, which decays exponentially with system size for any product state and non-trivial Hamiltonian. We propose quantum folding: for a system governed by a local Hamiltonian, seed the QSD with the product of the ground states of its subsystems, which differs from the target only through the interface terms. We prove a nonasymptotic error bound for the Chebyshev QSD that is linear in the measurement noise, by transplanting Kirby's effective-Hamiltonian analysis to the Chebyshev--Krylov basis, and identify the block-encoding rescaling of the Hamiltonian as a parameter of the guarantee. Exact simulations of antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chains show that the folded reference state reduces the Krylov dimension for a given accuracy severalfold and lowers the error under noise by two to five orders of magnitude relative to the N\'eel state. We show how the Ritz vector is prepared as a physical state and that the ground-state generation probability obeys a tight ceiling set by the overlap, so that recursive folding prepares ground states at polynomial cost. Taken together, these results allow for a scalable QSD framework that avoids the exponentially small ground-state overlaps associated with conventional product-state initialization. Finally we compute the fold fidelity itself: a slow power law for the gapless spin-1/2 chain, a size-independent constant for the gapped spin-$1$ chain, and an exact closed form converging to 1/4 for the AKLT chain.

items.title: Majorana Edge Modes Reshape Kibble-Zurek Scaling in Kitaev Honeycomb Ribbons
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hyesung Choi, Antonio Mandarino, Mahn-Soo Choi
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent progress in programmable quantum simulators motivates exact benchmarks for nonequilibrium dynamics in topological quantum matter. We study the Kitaev honeycomb model driven through its critical regions by a linear ramp of the bond coupling $J_z$ over a ramp time $\tau$, comparing zigzag and armchair ribbons with fully periodic tubes. The production of excitations exhibits a geometry-dependent finite-size crossover controlled by $N_2/\sqrt{\tau}$, the ratio of the ribbon width to the Kibble--Zurek length. Periodic tubes obey the expected critical-line Kibble--Zurek scaling and serve as the boundary-free benchmark. Zigzag ribbons follow the same scaling until defect production is exponentially suppressed by a finite-width algebraic gap floor associated with the formation of Majorana edge modes, whose occupation is pinned by inversion parity. Armchair ribbons instead support transient Majorana edge modes with exponentially small gaps, producing width-parity-dependent defect plateaus: exactly one defect per unit length for odd widths and an approximate, transient plateau near one half for even widths. The quench-generated entanglement entropy and fermionic logarithmic negativity inherit the same geometry-dependent structure, and the negativity further distinguishes the coherence-borne entanglement of the Kibble--Zurek regime from the population-borne entanglement of the edge-mode plateaus. These results identify boundary Majorana modes as the mechanism controlling departures from ideal Kibble--Zurek dynamics and provide geometry-resolved benchmarks for programmable simulations of topological matter.

items.title: A Reconstruction of Michelson Interference from On--Off Detection Statistics
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Kim Myung-Whun
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper reconstructs the Michelson interference phenomenon based solely on the binary (on-off) statistics of a single-photon counter and macroscopic path-difference data, without the a priori assumptions of complex wave superposition or prior spectral information. In contrast to the conventional approach that assumes light as a continuous complex wave function and considers interference between them, this study focuses on the algebraic properties inherent in discrete detection statistics. We verify that the discrete response data collected across various path differences form a positive semi-definite matrix, and apply Herglotz's theorem to this result. Consequently, we show that the harmonic form of the interference fringe is not a consequence of adopting a wave model as an axiom, but rather it is uniquely decomposed into a cosine average of wavenumbers dictated by testable algebraic constraints satisfied by the statistical data. Through this approach, the logical basis of the interference phenomenon can be described by the characteristics of the binary data itself, perfectly aligning with the modern optical experimental environment that relies entirely on discrete event statistics.

items.title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip for Superconducting Quantum Processor
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Rutian Huang, Xiao Geng, Xinyu Wu, Genting Dai, Liangliang Yang, Jianshe Liu, Wei Chen
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustable inductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.

items.author: Avadhut V. Purohit, Harshit Sharma, Udaysinh T. Bhosale
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong eigenstate thermalization (ETH) in operationally mean-ergodic, non-chaotic systems provides an opportunity to investigate whether Floquet eigenstates retain information about classical transport beyond their leading thermodynamic behavior. We address this question using the double kicked top (DKT), which exhibits nonmixing transport and dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport under variation of its control parameters. We show that the coefficient $m$ of the leading finite-size correction to the normalized eigenstate entanglement entropy (EE) $s$ tracks the restructuring between these transport regimes even when the thermodynamic-limit entropy $c$ becomes nearly insensitive to them. This coefficient $m$ is positive for nonmixing transport and negative when dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport dominate. The coefficient's sign reversal in the coexistence regime remains stable as the semiclassical resolution increases. Our results demonstrate that finite-size eigenstate structure can encode signatures of classical transport that are invisible in the thermodynamic-limit entropy, providing an eigenstate-based diagnostic of dynamical organization beyond the leading thermodynamic behavior associated with strong ETH.

We show that the coefficient $m$ of the leading finite-size correction to the normalized eigenstate entanglement entropy (EE) $s$ tracks the restructuring between these transport regimes even when the thermodynamic-limit entropy $c$ becomes nearly insensitive to them. This coefficient $m$ is positive for nonmixing transport and negative when dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport dominate. The coefficient's sign reversal in the coexistence regime remains stable as the semiclassical resolution increases. Our results demonstrate that finite-size eigenstate structure can encode signatures of classical transport that are invisible in the thermodynamic-limit entropy, providing an eigenstate-based diagnostic of dynamical organization beyond the leading thermodynamic behavior associated with strong ETH.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Arjen Vaartjes, Namit Anand, Rocky Y. Su, Akram Youssry, Ritik Sareen, Jeffrey Marshall, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Danielle Holmes, Benjamin Wilhelm, Bibek Pokharel, Xi Yu, Laura A. O'Neill, Martin Nurizzo, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. Itoh, Andrew S. Dzurak, David N. Jamieson, Andrea Morello
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.

items.title: Void-Free Through-Glass Vias for Multilayer Surface-Electrode Ion Traps
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Eike Iseke, Jacob Stupp, Friederike Giebel, Nila Krishnakumar, Konstantin Thronberens, Nora D. Stahr, Md. Masum Billah, Marlon Kuhn, Christian Ospelkaus
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Through-substrate interconnects are a key technology for scaling surface-electrode ion traps (SEITs) toward large electrode counts and complex architectures. Dielectric substrates such as fused silica offer superior RF performance compared to silicon, but the reliable fabrication of void-free through-glass vias (TGVs) remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate a SEIT fabricated on a fused silica substrate incorporating TGVs. The via-holes are formed using Selective Laser-Induced Etching and subsequently metallized with gold by electroplating. A patent-pending geometry-assisted bottom-up plating approach enables void-free filling using constant-current electroplating without electrolyte additives or pulsed deposition schemes. Electrical characterization across multiple wafers confirms a TGV-level yield above 98.8 %, demonstrating the robustness and reproducibility of the developed TGV technology. The TGVs are combined with multilayer SEIT fabrication, enabling vertical signal routing to all electrodes while maintaining an unaffected trapping surface without wire bonds. To interface the trap with external control electronics, a glass interposer providing signal fan-out to a larger pitch is designed and fabricated. The trap chip and the interposer are integrated using thermocompression bonding, forming a compact chip-to-chip assembly. The presented technology demonstrates the first fully integrated multilayer SEIT on fused silica incorporating void-free TGVs.

items.title: Quantum-enhanced phase interrogation of a fiber-optic strain sensor
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Romain Dalidet, Marialuisa Capezzuto, Hugo Degert, Davide D'Ambrosio, Saverio Avino, Anthony Martin, Sebastien Tanzilli, Laurent Labonte, Paolo De Natale, Gianluca Gagliardi
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fiber-optic sensors enable high-sensitivity measurements of various physical parameters. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enhanced interrogation of an all-fiber-optic Fabry-Perot resonator, employing entangled two-photon interference to probe directly strain-induced optical phase shifts. The resonator is interrogated by a narrow-linewidth laser that is frequency-locked to its resonance mode, thereby exploiting the cavity's inherent sensitivity to variations in the fiber length. To access the phase fluctuations transferred to the interrogation field due to external perturbations on the sensor, we implement an in-fiber Mach-Zehnder interferometer readout. This configuration allows the sensor to operate both with classical coherent light and with entangled photon pairs generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Harnessing two-photon entangled states corresponding to an N = 2 NOON state, we experimentally demonstrate a reduction of the measurement noise below the standard quantum limit. These results provide clear evidence of the quantum advantage in enhancing fiber-optic sensors under practical constraints on optical power.

items.title: Tomography for coherent noise
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Long Huang
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent noise poses a fundamentally greater challenge to quantum error correction than independent s- tochastic Pauli errors, because unitary errors preserve interference between error paths, can accumulate over multiple quantum error correction rounds, and leave the encoded logical channel with a residual coherent com- ponent. If the parameters of such coherent noise can be accurately determined, this knowledge can be exploited to inject correlated priors into the decoding graph, and to perform maximum-likelihood decoding under poly- nomially tractable structures, significantly improving the accuracy of syndrome-based decoding. In this work, we introduce one protocol to determine the model and parameters of coherent noise, and reduce the complexity of the experiment from 16nto O(16), which is of great significance for correcting coherent noise in quantum error correction.

items.title: Acoustic scattering from quantum dynamics
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Farhang Loran, Ali Mostafazadeh
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scattering of sound waves propagating in a compressible fluid is linked to the quantum dynamics generated by a class of non-Hermitian Hamiltonian operators. The scattering amplitude is expressed in terms of the corresponding evolution operator. This is used to provide a new proof of the reciprocity theorem in acoustic scattering, conduct analytic low-frequency acoustic scattering calculations, and study the scattering of sound waves by a finite planar array of delta-function point scatters embedded in an infinite acoustic slab. A detailed discussion of acoustic scattering properties of a homogeneous acoustic slab including a pair of delta-function point scatters on one of its faces is provided.

items.title: Selective Control and Imaging of Higgs and Goldstone Modes with a Quantum Simulator
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Connie Miao, Pranjal Praneel, Thomas G. Kiely, Eliott Rosenberg, Nicole S. Ticea, Pedram Roushan, Erich Mueller, Andre G. Petukhov
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We realize the mesoscopic Bose-Hubbard model at unit-filling on a two-dimensional array of transmon qubits and selectively excite collective modes associated with amplitude or phase fluctuations of the superfluid order parameter. We identify these modes respectively as the Higgs and Goldstone modes using complementary local observables, extracted from measuring the number of particles on each site. Modulation of the coupling between sites excites the Higgs mode, which we detect via the density of doubly occupied sites. In contrast, modulation of the local chemical potential with an appropriately chosen spatial profile excites the lowest-frequency Goldstone mode, which we detect via changes in the local density. The two modes have different symmetries and do not couple to one another. By varying the system geometry, we characterize the impact of finite system size on the evolution of both modes. In the thermodynamic limit, decay into a continuum of lower-energy excitations can obscure the Higgs response. In our mesoscopic system, however, the finite system size leads to spectral gaps and allows us to detect the Higgs mode as a coherent, long-lived excitation. Our work demonstrates how finite quantum simulators can isolate and probe physical phenomena that become difficult to resolve in the thermodynamic, large-scale limit.

items.title: Quantum-classical algorithm interpolation for spatial search
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Diogo Ramos, Duarte Magano
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum-walk algorithms can quadratically reduce the dependence of spatial search on the classical hitting time $\mathrm{HT}$. Realising this speedup using standard quantum-walk algorithms, however, requires deep coherent circuits, limiting their applicability on near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices. We derive a parameterised family of hybrid quantum-classical spatial search algorithms that continuously interpolates between the classical and fully coherent quantum regimes, trading off circuit depth for total query complexity. For any $\gamma\in[0,1]$, our algorithms use circuits of depth $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{HT}^{\gamma/2})$ and find a marked vertex with constant success probability at total cost $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{HT}^{1-\gamma}\mathsf{S} + \mathrm{HT}^{1-\gamma/2}(\mathsf{U} + \mathsf{C}))$, where $\mathsf{S}$, $\mathsf{U}$, and $\mathsf{C}$ denote the setup, update, and checking costs, respectively. We also derive an optimal continuous depth-query trade-off for fixed-point amplitude amplification, providing a potential building block for other hybrid designs.

items.title: Quantum Reservoir Computing for Attention-like Selective Reproduction
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Hadi Zadeh-Haghighi, Christoph Simon
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Choosing which information to use as the context changes is a basic cognitive operation. We introduce a new task of this kind for quantum reservoir computing (QRC): a binary cue indicates which of two simultaneous input streams the reservoir must reproduce. In simulated spin reservoirs with a trained linear readout, infinitely many measurements (exact expectation values) let the reservoir reproduce the cued stream accurately. At a finite number of measurements \(N_M\), the score exceeds that of a linear readout of the raw inputs only at large \(N_M\) because of sampling noise. Performance increases with both entanglement and coherence in the computational basis, and then saturates. These results show that QRC can select and reproduce a cued stream, and they are a starting point for harder cognitive tasks.

items.title: Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$-States: Dynamic $|T\rangle$ Post-Selection and Budget-Aware Factory Provisioning
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Maxwell Poster, Sayam Sethi, Yuhao Liu, Jonathan Baker, Costin Iancu
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magic $|T\rangle$-state preparation dominates the cost of fault-tolerant quantum computation on surface codes, yet cultivation and distillation are typically provisioned statically, leaving much of the program's error budget unused. We present Gap-Priced $|T\rangle$ States (GP$|T\rangle$-S), a lattice surgery scheduler and factory allocator that co-optimizes both methods under a total $T$-error budget. GP$|T\rangle$-S uses the complementary gap of each cultivated state as a fidelity estimate and dynamically adjusts the cultivation gap cutoff, converting budget slack into speed by giving the scheduler control over the cultivation post-selection. GP$|T\rangle$-S also characterizes distillation factories by size, $|T\rangle$-state production rate, and budget slack, and introduces cultivating factories that embed cultivation within routing channels, achieving fidelities otherwise requiring two-level distillation at a single-level footprint. GP$|T\rangle$-S organizes these characterizations into a factory catalog, and performs distillation factory allocation over this catalog in tandem with the gap cutoff using dynamic-programming to achieve one of i) minimum spacetime volume, ii) minimum execution time, or iii) minimum space overhead, all within a user-provided $T$-error budget. Across sixteen benchmarks under high and low $T$-error budgets of $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-5}$ respectively, GP$|T\rangle$-S consistently outperforms cultivation-only and single-factory baselines without exceeding the budget, achieving a 5.5$\times$ geometric mean speedup in logical cycle count and a 3.4$\times$ geometric mean reduction in space-time volume.

items.title: Leakage benchmarking with decohering subgroups in the presence of preparation and measurement errors
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Shawn Geller, Tongyu Zhao, Alex Kwiatkowski, Scott Glancy, Raymond W. Simmonds, Emanuel Knill
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A common problem with physical qubits is that the state can leak outside the computational subspace. To characterize the problem, it is desirable to measure both the leakage probability and the fidelity of gates inside the computational subspace. Randomized benchmarking is a readily accessible method for estimating average gate fidelities and can be modified to account for leakage. However, in the presence of state preparation and measurement errors (SPAM) there are parameter degeneracies, and fidelities and leakage become underdetermined. We study the example of qudits with any number of leakage levels under the assumption of gate-independent noise. We show that randomized benchmarking sequences with leakage level decoherence can be analyzed as a Markov process with noisy classical preparations and measurements. This result generalizes to randomized benchmarking with random gates from an arbitrary group that contains a phase-decohering subgroup. We characterize the parameter degeneracy in inferring the Markov process, preparations and measurements. Based on this characterization we develop a measurement and inference method taking advantage of known conservative bounds on SPAM to constrain fidelity, leakage and other parameters of the Markov process, state preparations and measurements. As part of our study, we experimentally implemented the measurement method for a qubit defined on the one-excitation subspace of two transmons, for which there are two leakage levels. We determined confidence intervals accounting for parameter degeneracy for a number of performance parameters of the system. For leakage and fidelity, we compare these intervals to those obtained for several conventional methods for leakage benchmarking.

items.title: Quantum LDPC Codes from Polynomial Minors
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Vahid Nourozi, Roxana Smarandache, David G. M. Mitchell
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct quantum codes from codewords of a cyclic code and the minors of a polynomial matrix. The construction uses a two-row, three-column matrix whose minors yield a second matrix satisfying the CSS orthogonality condition. We derive the code dimension from the greatest common divisors of the entries and minors, with a simplified formula for odd lifting factors. A residue characterization identifies additional common factors of the minors and leads to a method for controlling the dimension through polynomial selection. We also give a condition for changing the minor generator without changing the code. Explicit polynomial constructions yield 13 quantum codes with verified minimum distances, including a $[[255,80,12]]$ code of rate $80/255$.

items.title: Retrieving Metrological Information from Noisy Squeezed Spin States via Bayesian Optimization
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Enze Li, Yunjie Cai, Jingwei Zhang, Emi Yukawa
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency inhomogeneity can obscure the metrological advantage of squeezed spin states, making the choice of readout crucial. We study interacting spin-1/2 ensembles with static local frequency disorder and optimize a common collective readout over independent disorder realizations. Using Bayesian optimization of the full measurement-outcome distribution, we identify observables combining dipole and quadrupole operators that yield greater classical Fisher information than the optimized dipole readout considered here. For ensembles of up to 17 spins, their disorder-averaged CFI surpasses the standard quantum limit at both disorder strengths studied, including a regime where the dipole readout remains below it. For the larger ensembles studied, fixing the encoding axis to the direction that maximizes the disorder-averaged quantum Fisher information retains nearly the same performance. These results identify a route to extracting metrological information from frequency-disordered spin ensembles through the choice of collective observable.

items.title: Shot- and Noise-Aware Pauli Correlation Encoding for Max-Cut Experiments on IBM Heron Quantum Processor
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Achraf Boussahi
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pauli correlation encoding (PCE) encodes $m$ binary variables in the signs of $k$-body Pauli correlators of $n=O(m^{1/k})$ qubits, and trains a parameterized circuit on a relaxed loss of sharpness $\alpha$. The strongest published schedules sharpen this loss aggressively and are benchmarked with exact expectation values, whereas a quantum computer estimates correlators from a finite number of shots. We show that the sharpness is a hidden shot budget. Since the expected sign of a correlator estimated from $S$ shots, $\mathrm{erf}(c\sqrt{S/2})$, agrees with $\tanh(0.851\sqrt{S}\,c)$ to within $0.019$, the edge term of the relaxed loss at $\alpha=0.851\sqrt{S}$ approximately equals, up to a constant, minus twice the cut expected from decoding $S$ shots. This explains why schedules tuned with exact expectation values lose their advantage at realistic budgets, and yields a shot-aware schedule whose final sharpness is set by the shot budget. On five G-set graphs with $800$ variables on $13$ qubits, this schedule outperforms every published schedule at its target budget in all $150$ paired comparisons of the decoded circuit output, owing to the sharpness at $1.6\times10^4$ shots and mostly to switching off the regularization at $10^3$; after a classical bit-swap search, it remains the best on average at $1.6\times10^4$ shots. Device noise damps the correlators by a factor $s$, which amounts to a smaller shot budget $s^2S$. On the IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, an all-to-all ansatz of the type used for the best published G-set results compiles to $835$ CZ gates and decodes to a random cut, while our $96$-CZ hardware-native circuit, trained in simulation and sharpened to $\alpha\simeq0.65\,s\sqrt{S}$, retains up to $0.919$ of the best-known cut. For new circuits, a damping and an offset calibrated on other circuits of the same graph predicted the decoded cuts at $10^3$ shots to within $0.002$.

items.title: Logical gate set tomography
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Piper C. Wysocki, Juan Gonzalez De Mendoza, Karl Mayer, Natalie C. Brown, Ciaran Ryan-Anderson, Jalan A. Ziyad, Jordan H. Hines, Daniel G. Hothem, Corey I. Ostrove, Timothy J. Proctor, Kevin C. Young, Robin J. Blume-Kohout, Charles H. Baldwin, Kenneth M. Rudinger
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) can strongly suppress noise, but predicting whether a computation succeeds requires understanding not only how much effective noise persists after QEC, but what form that noise takes. To thoroughly characterize this noise, we introduce logical gate set tomography (``logical GST''). Logical GST produces detailed representations of noisy logical operations that can be used to derive higher-level metrics, such as gate fidelity and diamond distance, and to test for non-Markovian and coherent logical errors. We use logical GST to obtain the first full, self-consistent characterization of a universal single-qubit logical gate set, implemented in the seven-qubit Steane code using Quantinuum System Model H1, a 20-qubit trapped-ion quantum processor. In the experimental data from H1, logical GST identified predominantly logical Pauli-stochastic errors, found no evidence of logical non-Markovianity, and detected weak potential signatures of coherent logical error. By contrast, higher-shot datasets generated with Quantinuum's detailed system emulator, identify mechanisms for weak but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and strong evidence of coherent logical error. Finally, we use logical GST to perform error attribution with the system emulator, revealing how specific physical error sources shape logical error mechanisms.

items.title: The Generalized BEADS Representation: An Informationally Complete Visualization of Mixed Quantum States
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Celina Br\"autigam, Steffen J. Glaser, Dennis Huber
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A deep understanding of quantum information theory is essential for quantum science and technology. However, quantum mechanics and particularly quantum information theory suffer from a lack of intuitive images. Visualization tools offer novel perspectives on many problems in quantum physics by revealing important properties of quantum states and processes that are otherwise obscured by abstract mathematical formalisms. Here, we extend the previously established BEADS representation of pure states to the so-called generalized BEADS representation of mixed quantum states. We introduce spherical functions, so-called beads to visualize correlation structures of mixed quantum states. A recursive optimization scheme is used to obtain minimum-entanglement pure state decompositions of all subsystems of a given N-qubit state. We show how correlation function components can be decomposed into individual contributions that directly correspond to different types of correlations of mixed states. This allows us to visually characterize the total correlation, genuine n-partite entanglement, nonclassical quantum-discord-type correlations as well as classical correlations. After outlining the mathematical details relevant for constructing the representation, we examine the generalized BEADS representations for various classes of mixed states including product, classically correlated, separable but nonclassically correlated, as well as entangled states. As exemplary applications of the generalized BEADS representation, we showcase entanglement distillation and the effects of noise channels.

items.title: The cost of classically simulating quantum communication is as high as it could be
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Riccardo Castellano, Pavel Sekatski, Nicolas Brunner
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A long-standing open question is to characterize the classical communication cost of simulating the correlations arising from measurements on finite-dimensional quantum systems. We consider this question in the prepare-and-measure scenario. First we construct a classical simulation model involving a finite average number of bits of one-way communication that simulates exactly the correlations arising from arbitrary $d$-dimensional quantum states and arbitrary measurements. Second, we show that no classical simulation protocol involving a finite average message dimension can exist for $d\geq 4$, hence strengthening a recent result of de Gois, Santos and Vieira. Our first result relies on a more general simulation theorem which can be applied to certain continuous variable (i.e. infinite-dimensional) quantum systems, and even beyond quantum theory, e.g. to generalized probabilistic theories. In particular, we show that multimode Gaussian states of bounded average energy and general Gaussian measurements admit an exact classical simulation with a finite expected number of bits. Overall, our results show that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially as high as it could be.

items.title: A modular quantum computer based on Cornucopia codes
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zhide Lu, Weikang Li, Yinghao Ma, Hanyu Yan, Bingrun Wang, Yixuan Ma, Zheng-Zhi Sun, Dong-Ling Deng
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultra-high-rate quantum error correction codes can store many logical qubits in a single code block with few physical qubits. A fault-tolerant quantum computer, however, also requires a universal set of logical operations on individually addressable logical qubits, and the ancilla overhead of these operations may erode the advantage of the high encoding rate. Here, we propose the Cornucopia architecture, in which a universal set of logical operations is implemented at low overhead for the Cornucopia codes. In particular, we focus on the [[2844,1426,18]] Cornucopia code as an example and introduce a modular quantum computer built from such code blocks connected by bridges. Each block stores 1,426 logical qubits and serves as a universal logical processor. Exploiting the code's translation symmetry, we construct a family of reusable gadgets that individually address 1,422 logical qubits within each block. These gadgets support three universal logical instruction sets: basic, high-throughput and fixed-extractor. Excluding magic-state factories, a module with sufficient workspace to execute any instruction in the basic set requires an average of 4.1 physical qubits per logical qubit, compared with 3.0 for memory alone. The architecture thus preserves the resource advantage of ultra-high-rate quantum memory while enabling universal logical computation, providing a route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computers.

items.title: Federated Unlearning of Quantum Data via Classical Shadows
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Zihao Ding, Jun Huang, Cong-cong Xing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum federated learning trains a quantum neural network (QNN) across nodes that hold quantum data, such as the states of quantum sensors. To forget data, unlearning methods for quantum models replay them, and federated unlearning from stored updates removes whole nodes only. Quantum data cannot be replayed, since a state is consumed when measured and cannot be cloned. We propose Shadow-based Data Erasure (SHADE), in which each node records a classical shadow of every training state, a few randomized single-qubit measurements taken at training time. The gradient and curvature of a QNN on a state are expectations of observables, so SHADE estimates them for the forget data from the shadows at any later parameters and removes their effect by a federated Newton correction. Only classical estimates cross the network. We prove that the shadow size needed for a target unlearning error grows exponentially in the size of the backward light cone of the measured observable and not in the number of qubits. In simulation with 50 nodes and on edge boards, SHADE matches the forget accuracy of retraining within 0.5 points, without replay and in under 0.2 s.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Prince Frederick Kwao, Bharath Sambasivam, Jason Saroni, Srivathsan Poyyapakkam Sundar, Edwin Barnes, Ayush Asthana
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Circuit depth and measurement count are the main limitations for chemical applications of the leading variational quantum algorithms on quantum computers. We show that both resource requirements can be reduced by augmenting adaptive variational quantum algorithms with post-optimization corrective techniques. We focus on two such techniques---Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization and the identity-augmented quantum self-consistent equation of motion (q-sc-EOM)---applied to optimized ADAPT-VQE states without further ansatz growth or nonlinear optimization. Across molecular systems studied with up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduces the optimized iterations (and the corresponding number of adaptive layers) needed to reach the $1.6~\mathrm{m}E_h$ threshold by up to approximately sixfold, with a general trend toward larger reductions at higher determinant R\'enyi entropy. We also find measurement-cost reductions of up to approximately fortyfold using a suitable resource-cost model. Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM improves molecular potential-energy curves obtained from truncated ADAPT-VQE ans\"atze with limited expressivity and recovers accuracy from states produced by sampled operator ranking without additional gradient-based operator selection, providing an advantage when small pool gradients make selection measurement intensive. Together, these post-optimization corrections offer routes to improve energy accuracy and reduce adaptive circuit growth in quantum algorithms as quantum hardware advances.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Tristan Lorriaux, Yutian Wen, Patrice Bertet, Benjamin Huard, Audrey Bienfait
items.summary: arXiv:2610.19180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic nuclear polarisation transfers polarisation from electron to nuclear spins by relying on a dissipative channel. Here we introduce a cavity-based DNP mechanism which uses the radiative relaxation of the electronic spin through the Purcell effect to bring about the nuclear spin polarisation. We implement this protocol on an ensemble of bismuth donor spins (I=9/2, S=1/2) in isotopically purified silicon coupled to a superconducting resonator. A single cycle, combining adiabatic microwave and radio-frequency pulses with Purcell relaxation, increases a target ground state's population by a factor of $1.79\pm0.04$; a cumulative enhancement of $4.6\pm0.2$ is reached with additional cycles, to be compared with the theoretical limit of ninefold set by the degeneracy of the ground manifold. We explain this difference by the competition between Purcell and intrinsic relaxation on the one hand and a collective effect that slows down the electronic spin radiative decay as the nuclear spin population grows on the other hand. Our results place radiative DNP as an available mechanism at millikelvin temperatures where phonon-mediated relaxation is frozen.

items.title: Optimal Disorder Strength for Approximate Unitary $k$-Designs in Spin Chains
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Tian-Gang Zhou, Yi-Neng Zhou, Thierry Giamarchi, Julian Sonner
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum simulators with disordered spin Hamiltonians offer a natural route to Haar-like unitary ensembles, but face a competition. Disorder enhances randomness, yet strong disorder suppresses dynamics and localizes the system in the computational basis. This suggests an optimal intermediate disorder strength for approximating a unitary $k$-design, which has so far been identified mainly empirically. Here, we develop a perturbative theory for the moment gap $\Delta^{(k)}$, the deviation of the $k$-th moment operator from its Haar value, for the full spectrum of the interacting XXZ chain in a fixed-magnetization sector. We find the non-monotonic asymptotic scalings $\ln \Delta^{(k)}\sim -\sigma^2$ at weak disorder and $\ln \Delta^{(k)}\sim -1/\sigma$ at strong disorder, whose crossover sets an optimal disorder strength $\sigma_c\sim J_{xy}$, where $J_{xy}$ is the energy scale of the non-random interaction. We further show that a multi-quench protocol further suppresses the gap exponentially in the number of quenches. Numerical simulations confirm both scalings and this exponential suppression, and we demonstrate the usefulness of the protocol for classical shadow tomography. This work suggests that strong disorder may block both thermalization and the formation of unitary designs through a common localization mechanism.

items.title: Stabilizer R\'enyi Entropy Without a Phase Reference
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Jinwei Chu, Savan Kharel
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stabilizer R\'enyi entropy quantifies magic relative to a complete Pauli frame. In settings such as helicity states of massless particles, unsynchronized qubit registers, energy eigenbases, and systems under superselection rules, the computational basis may be fixed while the transverse Pauli axes remain unspecified. The stabilizer R\'enyi entropy then depends on the choice of those axes. We define a phase-averaged stabilizer R\'enyi entropy by averaging the Pauli moments before taking the logarithm. It is exactly invariant under independent local rephasings. For pure states, it vanishes precisely when the state is a stabilizer state in every phase convention. For a broad class of sparse supports, it reduces to a closed-form function of the basis-state probabilities alone. Within this class, the ceiling for $n$ channels is $\ln[n^{3}/(6n-5)]$ for $n\geq3$ and $\ln\frac{7}{5}$ for two channels. We apply the invariant to tree-level gluon scattering at four and five points, where the helicity-basis phases are unspecified. It saturates the two- and three-channel ceilings: $\ln\frac{7}{5}$ at four points and $\ln\frac{27}{13}$ in $3\to2$ scattering. In same-helicity $2\to3$ scattering, it lies between a floor of $\ln\frac{8}{7}$ and a ceiling of $\ln\frac{184}{125}$, reached in the resolved soft limit and particular collinear limits, respectively. In every configuration studied, the invariant is independent of the fixed external colors.

items.title: Programmable Polaron Models and Tomography in Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulators
items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Filip Marijanovic, Utso Bhattacharya, Abhishek Menon, Visal So, Guido Pagano, Eugene Demler
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong coupling between mobile charge carriers or excitons and lattice vibrations gives rise to polarons: quasiparticles formed by charge carriers dressed by a cloud of phonon excitations. Polaron formation determines transport properties of systems ranging from transition-metal oxides and organic semiconductors to light-harvesting complexes. In excitonic systems that admit a hard-core boson description, mapping the excitations to pseudospins provides a natural framework for studying polaron physics, including the nonperturbative regime in which hopping amplitudes, phonon energies, and coupling strengths are comparable. Here, we propose a trapped-ion blueprint for realizing spin-phonon Hamiltonians with programmable spatial coupling between excitation density and phonon displacements, encompassing local Holstein and long-range Fr\"ohlich-type interactions. To access strongly dressed quasiparticles whose bare spectral weight is suppressed, we introduce displaced Green's functions implemented through spin-dependent phonon displacements. Their spectral response reveals the polaron band spectrum, including binding energies and phonon-excitation sidebands, while spatially resolved measurements probe the structure of the phonon dressing cloud, providing a route to polaron tomography. We further complement this spectroscopy with direct and ancilla-assisted measurements of spin-phonon correlations that track the coupled dynamics of the excitation and its environment. These approaches connect the emergent quasiparticle spectrum to the microscopic buildup of its dressing cloud, enabling controlled studies of how the spatial range of coupling shapes polaron formation and mobility.

items.subtitle: ARXIV · QUANT-PH · PREPRINT SIGNAL
items.author: Amir-Reza Negari, Yijian Zou, Timothy H. Hsieh
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under local Lindbladian evolution, the growth of conditional mutual information and its associated Markov length scale is not limited by Lieb-Robinson bounds, yet it has been unclear how quickly the Markov length can increase. We show that an arbitrarily short, strictly local Lindbladian can generate infinite Markov length from a product state. We also construct strictly local Lindbladians that converge rapidly to steady states with algebraically decaying conditional mutual information. Despite their long-range conditional correlations, the states we construct are local reversibly connected to a product state by sublinear depth circuits. Thus infinite Markov length does not imply slow relaxation nor obstruct phase stability when suitably defined.
